new_statements.quote: Content words contain at least two vowels. Some functors, such as the conjunction ma ‘and’, are monosyllabic. Stress falls on the penultimate vowel of a word with secondary stress assigned to every second syllable to the left.
new_statements.citation: Edwards, Owen. 2021. Rote-Meto Comparative Dictionary. Canberra: ANU Press (Asia-Pacific Linguistics).
new_statements.locator: sec. 2.4.1 'Rote' (Language background), printed p. 35 = PDF p. 47
new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary stress on the penultimate vowel of the word; secondary stress on every second vowel to the left of it (alternating trochaic pattern from the right). Since double vowels (VV) are phonetically long and one member of any vowel sequence is always stressed, a word-final double vowel surfaces as final stress on a long vowel (cf. Jonker 1915: 5-6, final accent on derivatives of monosyllabic roots).
new_statements.secondary_stress: Stated: 'secondary stress assigned to every second syllable to the left' (same wording for Termanu on p. 12).
new_statements.exceptions: Monosyllabic functors (e.g. ma 'and') fall outside the disyllabic minimum; the nominal enclitic =a (Landu entry, p. 88) does not attract stress: 'Stress remains on the penultimate syllable of the host', the enclitic often being non-syllabic in citation form. Jonker 1915: 5-6 (Termanu) adds final accent on derivatives/compounds whose last member is a monosyllabic (long-vowel) root.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level statement made for the Rote languages as a group (sec. 2.4.1 covers all Rote lects, Rikou included) in a comparative dictionary's phonological overview, not a Rikou-specific description. Edwards has his own Rikou field data (Nov 2017; Table 1.2) and in Edwards 2018: 365-366 transcribes Rikou uraʔ [ˈʔʊraʔ], ʔuse-ʔ [ˈʔʊsɛʔ], au ʔuseʔ [ˌʔawˈʔʊsɛʔ] with penultimate primary and alternating secondary stress, consistent with the rule.
new_statements.identity_note: The quoted statement is made for the Rote languages collectively (Edwards 2021 sec. 2.4.1), which include Rikou/Ringgou with its dialects Landu and Oepao (= ring1244 [rgu]; Edwards's Table 2.2 lists Rikou proper as nucl1538, Landu as land1257, Oepao as oepa1237). It is not a Ringgou-specific phonological description; Edwards's Rikou field data and his stress-marked Rikou transcriptions (Edwards 2018: 365-366) are the Rikou-specific support. Jonker 1915's parallel rule is Termanu (term1237/pada1259)-based.

sources.citation: Jonker, J. C. G. 1915. Rottineesche Spraakkunst. Leiden: Brill. xxiv+714 pp.
sources.note: Sec. 4 'De Klemtoon', printed pp. 5-6 (scan pp. 33-34): accent falls 'steeds op de vóór-laatste lettergreep' in di-/trisyllabic stems; final in derivatives of monosyllabic roots and compounds ending in one (long vowel); secondary accent on 3rd/4th syllable from the end; 'Verspringing van den klemtoon komt... niet voor' under pronominal enclitics. Grammar treats mainly Termanu; Ringgou is named p. 1 among the dialects (k-loss noted) but the stress section is not dialect-specific.

Rikou forms are transcribed with penultimate stress, pp. 365-366: 'Rikou uraʔ [ˈʔʊraʔ] scorpion and ʔuse-ʔ [ˈʔʊsɛʔ] navel', 'au ʔuseʔ [ˌʔawˈʔʊsɛʔ] my navel'; fn. 8 p. 366 notes Jonker's accents mark vowel quality and 'the placement of stress'.

sources.citation: Jonker, J. C. G. 1913. Bijdrage tot de kennis der Rottineesche tongvallen. Bijdragen tot de Taal-, Land- en Volkenkunde van Nederlandsch-Indië 68: 521-622. doi:10.1163/22134379-90001774
sources.note: Dialect survey (pp. 521-536) plus translated and original texts in the nine Rote dialects including Ringgou and an Oepao piece. The only occurrence of 'klemtoon' is p. 521 (the name Manafè 'met den klemtoon op de laatste lettergreep'); pp. 532-533 characterise Ringgou by ngg > k, initial nd > r, irregular hiatus, closeness to Bilba. Silent on Ringgou word stress.
